captureMethod: Read actual Unity Game View / graph GUI render surfaces; normalize vertical pixel origin for Metal. No fabricated scene or HUD content.

steps: Open Campfire/Demo.unity without saving changes.
Set temporary Game View fixed resolution to 1920x1080.
Enter Play Mode and wait for the manager to be ready.
Keep the fire unlit.
captures.alt: Campfire before ignition, with the Ready for a spark readout and Ignite fire button.
captures.caption: Before ignition, no Campfire play is active.

steps: Invoke CampfireInteraction.ToggleFire, equivalent to the F/button control.
Wait until ignition completes and the crackling loop fades in.
captures.alt: Voxel flames rise from the Campfire island with Burning bright and Extinguish fire in the HUD.
captures.caption: The ignition has completed and the selected crackle recording loops.

steps: Start with the lit state.
Temporarily hide runtime UIDocument roots.
Read the composed Game View render texture.
Restore UIDocument visibility.
captures.alt: A lit voxel campfire on its grassy island, captured in Unity with the HUD temporarily hidden.
captures.caption: A clean Unity Game View image for the home-page hero.

steps: Exit Play Mode.
Open Campfire.soundgraph in Unity.
Maximize its editor tab, hide the audition overlay, and frame all nodes.
Capture the GUI view render surface with GrabPixels.
Close the temporary graph tab and restore the previous Game View settings.
captures.alt: Unity Campfire graph showing ignition, crackle selection, Intensity, and release connections.
captures.caption: The authored Campfire graph, captured from its own Unity editor GUI render surface.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/02-Footstep/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Walk left with A until you reach the grass lane.
Let at least one grass step register, then stop near the middle of the lane.
captures.alt: Footstep in Unity: a step on grass. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The player stands in the grass lane after a grass footfall. Each step uses the Surface value to choose a material, then a short variation from that recording.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/02-Footstep/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
From the center spawn, walk right a short distance with D while staying in the stone lane.
Let one stone step register, then release D.
captures.alt: Footstep in Unity: a step on stone. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The middle lane uses stone footsteps. The same Sounds.Footstep key is used for all three surfaces; the parameter changes which branch supplies the sound.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/02-Footstep/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Hold D to cross the middle stone lane into the wood lane.
Continue until a wood step registers, then stop.
captures.alt: Footstep in Unity: a step on wood. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The player has crossed into the wood lane. Compare the surface readout with the grass and stone views.

steps: Exit Play Mode.
In Unity’s Project window, double-click Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/02-Footstep/Footstep.soundgraph.
Use the mouse wheel to zoom and drag the graph background to bring the relevant nodes into view.
Frame the entire graph for an overview. Use the close views on this page for small labels.
captures.alt: Footstep in Unity: the complete Footstep graph. The graph nodes and their connections are visible.
captures.caption: Three groups prepare grass, stone, and wood variations. A surface selector chooses one group for each footfall.

captures.alt: Footstep in Unity: grass variations. The graph nodes and their connections are visible.
captures.caption: Four Wave Asset nodes use different start times and lengths from Footsteps_Grass. Random Clip chooses one of those short sections.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/03-Bee/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Leave the bee resting on its flower.
captures.alt: Bee in Unity: ready to fly. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The bee rests on its flower. The listener is at the player in the center, so the distance readout measures from there.

captures.state: The bee passes on the right
steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/03-Bee/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Press Space or choose Release bee.
Wait for the bee to fly to the right side of the player.
captures.alt: Bee in Unity: the bee passes on the right. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The bee is flying on the right side of the listener. The demo starts one looping buzz with a context that follows the bee Transform.

captures.state: The bee passes on the left
steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/03-Bee/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Press Space or choose Release bee.
Let the bee continue around the player until it reaches the left side.
captures.alt: Bee in Unity: the bee passes on the left. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The same flight continues around the player. Following the Transform updates the sound position as the bee moves; it does not start a new buzz each frame.

steps: Exit Play Mode.
In Unity’s Project window, double-click Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/03-Bee/Bee.soundgraph.
Use the mouse wheel to zoom and drag the graph background to bring the relevant nodes into view.
Frame the entire graph for an overview. Use the close views on this page for small labels.
captures.alt: Bee in Unity: one buzz with a changing speed. The graph nodes and their connections are visible.
captures.caption: On Start begins the looping bee clip. WingSpeed controls its playback speed. The moving position comes from the play context supplied by the demo script.

steps: Exit Play Mode.
In Unity’s Project window, select Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/03-Bee/Bee.soundgraph.
In the Inspector, expand Spatial audio. Read the values shown here; no changes are needed.
captures.alt: Bee in Unity: make the buzz a 3D sound. The saved event values are visible in the Inspector.
captures.caption: Spatial blend is 1, with linear distance falloff from 0.8 to 4 world units and Doppler set to 0.3. These are the event settings used by the moving bee.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/04-Engine/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Start the engine and leave the throttle at zero.
Wait for ignition to finish and the readout to settle near 950 RPM.
captures.alt: Engine in Unity: the engine idles. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The engine is running at about 950 RPM with no throttle. The scene keeps the Engine play available for changing parameters and receiving signals.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/04-Engine/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Start the engine and raise the throttle slider to 92%.
Let the car accelerate for several seconds.
captures.alt: Engine in Unity: more throttle, higher RPM. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The throttle is at 92% and the engine has climbed above 6,000 RPM. The demo updates Rpm and Load while the engine layers continue playing.

captures.state: A horn and a gear change
steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/04-Engine/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Start the engine, raise the throttle, and let the car accelerate.
Use the Shift and Horn controls while the engine keeps running. Capture during the short cues.
captures.alt: Engine in Unity: a horn and a gear change. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The car is now in second gear after the Shift and Horn signals. Their short sounds can play alongside the engine loops.

steps: Exit Play Mode.
In Unity’s Project window, double-click Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/04-Engine/Engine.soundgraph.
Use the mouse wheel to zoom and drag the graph background to bring the relevant nodes into view.
Frame the entire graph for an overview. Use the close views on this page for small labels.
captures.alt: Engine in Unity: the complete Engine graph. The graph nodes and their connections are visible.
captures.caption: The groups separate ignition, running layers, Horn and Shift signals, and the shutdown sound.

steps: Exit Play Mode.
In Unity’s Project window, double-click Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/04-Engine/Engine.soundgraph.
Use the mouse wheel to zoom and drag the graph background to bring the relevant nodes into view.
Find the nodes described under “Turn RPM into sound controls” on this page and zoom in to read their fields and connections.
captures.alt: Engine in Unity: turn RPM into sound controls. The graph nodes and their connections are visible.
captures.caption: The normalized Rpm value changes playback speed and the balance of the engine layers. Remap Float converts its 0–1 input into the range needed by the sound.

steps: Exit Play Mode.
In Unity’s Project window, double-click Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/04-Engine/Engine.soundgraph.
Use the mouse wheel to zoom and drag the graph background to bring the relevant nodes into view.
Find the nodes described under “Add the engine load” on this page and zoom in to read their fields and connections.
captures.alt: Engine in Unity: add the engine load. The graph nodes and their connections are visible.
captures.caption: Load passes through a remapping node and is multiplied with the layer's volume control. This lets throttle affect the sound without starting a new event.

steps: Exit Play Mode.
In Unity’s Project window, double-click Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/04-Engine/Engine.soundgraph.
Use the mouse wheel to zoom and drag the graph background to bring the relevant nodes into view.
Find the nodes described under “Respond to Horn and Shift” on this page and zoom in to read their fields and connections.
captures.alt: Engine in Unity: respond to Horn and Shift. The graph nodes and their connections are visible.
captures.caption: Each On Signal node triggers a short cue. The running engine does not need to stop for either signal.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/05-Weather/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Leave the skies clear without starting a weather session.
captures.alt: Weather in Unity: before the rain. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The island is dry and the weather session is stopped. This gives a quiet starting point for comparison with the storm.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/05-Weather/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Choose the Storm preset.
Wait for rain to reach 100% and wind to reach 85%.
captures.alt: Weather in Unity: a full storm. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The Storm preset has brought rain to 100% and wind to 85%. The demo changes the sound parameters and the scene's visual effects together.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/05-Weather/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Choose Storm and wait for the Thunder control to become available.
Trigger Thunder and capture the first flash immediately. This frame was recorded about 0.08 seconds after the strike.
captures.alt: Weather in Unity: the first lightning flash. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: This is the actual flash, captured about 0.08 seconds after the strike. The demo creates the light and bolt immediately; the Thunder graph delays its sound. The HUD counter updates separately and still shows the previous count in this frame.

captures.alt: Weather in Unity: the Weather graph. The graph nodes and their connections are visible.
captures.caption: Rain and wind have their own groups. Parameters shape continuous layers while the weather session is running.

Use the mouse wheel to zoom and drag the graph background to bring the relevant nodes into view.

captures.alt: Weather in Unity: the Thunder graph. The graph nodes and their connections are visible.
captures.caption: A delay separates the flash from its rumble. Random Clip chooses a thunder variation, and the event ends after playback finishes.

steps: Exit Play Mode.
In Unity’s Project window, double-click Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/05-Weather/Weather.soundgraph.

captures.caption: This frame records a hammer impact while Handsaw remains selected and working. The tap button is briefly unavailable during the tap itself, then becomes available again.

captures.alt: Arcade in Unity: sounds compete for space. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: At 100% Chaos, the counters show accepted, replaced, and limited requests. The exact totals vary each run; here the cooldown counter is still zero.

captures.alt: Arcade in Unity: zap variations. The graph nodes and their connections are visible.

steps: Exit Play Mode.

captures.alt: Arcade in Unity: replace an older zap. The saved event values are visible in the Inspector.

steps: Exit Play Mode.

captures.alt: Arcade in Unity: reject an extra coin play. The saved event values are visible in the Inspector.
captures.caption: ArcadeCoin allows two overlapping instances and uses Reject New. Existing coin sounds can finish when another request arrives at the limit.

steps: Exit Play Mode.
In Unity’s Project window, select Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/07-Arcade/ArcadeJackpot.soundgraph.

captures.alt: Arcade in Unity: leave a gap between jackpots. The saved event values are visible in the Inspector.
captures.caption: ArcadeJackpot has a three-second cooldown: requests made too soon after an accepted play are refused.

steps: Exit Play Mode.
In Unity’s Project window, select Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/07-Arcade/ArcadeJackpot.soundgraph.
In the Inspector, expand Concurrency & priority. Read the values shown here; no changes are needed.
captures.alt: Arcade in Unity: protect the jackpot cue. The saved event values are visible in the Inspector.
captures.caption: ArcadeJackpot allows one instance, uses Reject New, and has priority 32 with Protected enabled. Lower priority numbers are more important.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/10-Launch/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Leave Auto selected and the launch stopped at Mission Control.
captures.alt: Launch in Unity: ready at Mission Control. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The pad is stopped with Auto selected. No voices are playing yet.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/10-Launch/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Choose Manual, then Launch.
Set power to 100% and leave the clamps closed. Wait for PRESSURE WARNING.
captures.alt: Launch in Unity: too much pressure in Manual. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: Power is at 100% with the clamps still closed. The PRESSURE WARNING status is active; the large Ready for the sky line is the demo's normal preparing-phase readout.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/10-Launch/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Choose Manual, start the launch, and raise power to 100% with the clamps closed.
Wait for the pressure warning, then choose Abort. Capture the safe-shutdown state.
captures.alt: Launch in Unity: abort the launch. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The manual launch has been aborted. The scene reports a safe shutdown while the ending audio finishes.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/10-Launch/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Leave Auto selected and choose Launch.
Let the controller power the pad, vent pressure, and open the clamps. Capture when the countdown displays 3.
captures.alt: Launch in Unity: three seconds to liftoff. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: Auto has supplied enough power, reduced pressure, and opened the clamps. The graph can now begin its three-count sequence.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/10-Launch/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.
Leave Auto selected and choose Launch.
Allow countdown and ignition to finish. Capture shortly after liftoff while the rocket is still above the pad.
captures.alt: Launch in Unity: the rocket lifts off. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The rocket is just above the pad with its thrusters active. The flight event follows the moving rocket.

steps: In Unity’s Project window, open Assets/DEV505/SoundManager/Samples/10-Launch/Demo.unity. Enter Play Mode and click the Game view so it receives your keyboard input.

captures.alt: Launch in Unity: pause during flight. The real scene controls and status readouts are visible.
captures.caption: The rocket is held at the same altitude and the HUD reports LAUNCH PAUSED. The demo pauses its motion and retained audio plays together.
